title: The case for Mark 16:9-20
subtitle: The Longer Ending stood as Scripture in the Greek manuscript tradition, the Lectionaries, and the Fathers.
summary: External support across 99% of the Greek manuscripts, the Old Latin and Syriac versions, and Irenaeus, Tatian, Justin, and Hippolytus, set against the narrow case from Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, and Eusebius. A defense of the Longer Ending on patristic and manuscript grounds.
origin: Discord, dogma-exegesis: The Case for Mark 16:9-20.

essay.text: The Longer Ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) is one of the most contested passages in modern textual criticism. Its absence from two famous early Greek manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, is the standing argument that the verses are a later addition. The case is taken to settle the matter; in fact, it does not.

Mark 16:9-20 is supported by over 99% of the Greek manuscripts of the Gospel of Mark, by over thirty (closer to forty) early patristic references, and by a wide range of versional witnesses, Latin, Syriac, Gothic, Coptic. Out of roughly 1,650 Greek manuscripts of Mark, only three end at 16:8; one of those three is a medieval commentary in which the same commentator's longer work treats verses 9-20. The Longer Ending is the normal form of the text from its initial production at Rome onward.
The early manuscripts that stop at v. 8

Codex Vaticanus (B) stops at v. 8, but leaves an entire blank column after it. This is "memorial space": a scribe who knew his exemplar was missing something marked the gap with empty parchment. Codex Sinaiticus (Aleph) also stops at v. 8, with a replacement four-leaf bifolium in its own ending. Both are fourth-century Egyptian-tradition manuscripts; both carry physical signs that the scribes were aware of an ending they could not include from their exemplars. Outside Egypt, the verses are everywhere.
Eusebius does not know the Shorter Ending

The objection from Eusebius of Caesarea (Ad Marinum) is often cited; less often noticed is what Eusebius does not say. He shows no awareness of the so-called Shorter Ending, the alternative two-sentence ending that appears in a handful of late Egyptian manuscripts. If the Shorter Ending had been a known variant in the early fourth century at Caesarea, a scholar of Eusebius' caliber would have mentioned it. He does not, because the ending that was disputed in his circle was the Longer Ending preserved in the wider Church, not a competing shorter form.
The patristic chain in the second century

Mark 16:9-20 is attested by at least four second-century witnesses, more than a hundred years before Vaticanus and Sinaiticus. Justin Martyr (c. 155) uses in his First Apology a phrase, ἐξελθόντες πανταχοῦ ἐκήρυξαν ("going out, they preached everywhere"), which occurs nowhere else in the surviving Greek of any author except Mark 16:20. Tatian's Diatessaron (172) wove the four Gospels into one harmony and included the twelve verses. The Epistula Apostolorum (c. 150) echoes the narrative shape of the Longer Ending. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 184) quotes Mark 16:19 by name in Book III of Against Heresies.
The manuscript notes that defend the passage

Where later Greek manuscripts contain marginal notes about Mark 16:9-20, they almost always defend the passage rather than impugn it. Manuscripts 20, 215, and 300, with the Jerusalem Colophon, carry a note that reads: "From here to the end forms no part of the text in some of the copies. But in the ancient ones, it all appears intact." The scribes are reporting that they knew of late copies missing the ending, but that the older copies they consulted contained it whole.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: His apostles, going forth from Jerusalem, preached everywhere, ἐξελθόντες πανταχοῦ ἐκήρυξαν, that the things which had been declared by them concerning Jesus Christ were certainly true.
florilegium.gloss: The Greek participle-and-verb pair occurs nowhere else in surviving Greek literature except Mark 16:20. Justin was citing a text he held in his hands, c. 200 years before Vaticanus.

florilegium.author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
florilegium.text: Also, towards the conclusion of his Gospel, Mark says: "So then, after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was received up into heaven, and sits on the right hand of God."
florilegium.gloss: Irenaeus quotes Mark 16:19 by name. A Greek annotation in Codex 1582 next to Mark 16:19 affirms this citation: "Irenaeus, who lived near the time of the Apostles, cites this from Mark in the third book of his work Against Heresies."

florilegium.author: Tatian the Assyrian
florilegium.text: Then went forth those eleven into all the regions of Galilee, in the days of the feast, into the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, and when they saw him there, they worshipped him… And he upbraided them for their lack of faith, and the hardness of their hearts, in that they believed not those who saw him after he was risen.
florilegium.gloss: Tatian's harmony absorbs Mark 16:14 and the following verses into a unified Gospel narrative. The Longer Ending was treated as canonical Scripture alongside the other three Gospels by the mid-second century.

florilegium.author: St Hippolytus of Rome
florilegium.work: Apostolic Tradition (and material in Apostolic Constitutions VIII)
florilegium.text: Let every one of the believers be sure to partake of communion before he eats anything else. For if he partakes with faith, even if something deadly were given to him, after this it cannot hurt him.
florilegium.gloss: A direct allusion to Mark 16:18. The Apostolic Constitutions, which incorporate Hippolytan material, then quote Mark 16:16-18 in extenso at the head of Book VIII.

florilegium.author: Author of the Didascalia Apostolorum
florilegium.text: To every one therefore who believes and is baptized his former sins have been forgiven. … We had divided the whole world into twelve parts, and were gone forth among the Gentiles into all the world to preach the word.
florilegium.gloss: The Didascalia echoes Mark 16:15-16 in chapters 20 and 23. The Longer Ending was already shaping early Syriac church order.

florilegium.author: Vincentius of Thibaris
florilegium.work: Statement at the Seventh Council of Carthage
florilegium.text: We have assuredly the rule of truth which the Lord by his divine precept commanded to his Apostles, saying, "Go ye, lay on hands in my name, expel demons." And in another place: "Go ye and teach," etc.
florilegium.gloss: A North African bishop, at a conciliar session in 256, cites Mark 16:15-18 as the apostolic mandate. The Longer Ending was the conciliar text of the third-century African Church.

florilegium.author: James Snapp Jr
florilegium.work: Authentic Case for Mark 16:9-20, Fourth Edition
florilegium.text: Out of about 1,650 Greek manuscripts of the Gospel of Mark, only three Greek manuscripts end the text at 16:8. Two of those three are early. These two early copies, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, represent a form of the text of Mark which circulated in Egypt in the early 200s and was taken from there to the city of Caesarea, where it was still found in the 300s. Although the text of Mark in Codex Vaticanus stops at 16:8, the copyist left a clear indication that he recollected the absent verses: after Mark 16:8, there is a distinct blank space in Codex Vaticanus, including an entire blank column. This is an example of "memorial space."
florilegium.gloss: Modern textual scholarship's case for the Longer Ending, as a summary of the manuscript record.

scripture.note: Go ye into all the world, the Great Commission as Mark records it.
He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved.
They shall take up serpents, cited by Hippolytus, the Apostolic Constitutions, and the Didascalia.
Quoted by Irenaeus in Against Heresies III.10.
Quoted in unique Greek phrasing by Justin Martyr.
Paired with Mark 16:15-18 in the conciliar citation of Vincentius.
